item.title: Stop Blaming Remote Work for Sloppy Communication Habits
item.description:
Productivity

Stop Blaming Remote Work for Sloppy Communication Habits

We can experience the pros of working remotely without sacrificing effectiveness.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Remote workers report higher well-being scores and lower turnover rates than in-office employees.
  • Despite that, many organization are mandating a return to office work to improve performance.
  • The real problem, research shows, is clumsy asynchronous communication.
  • With a few optimizations, teams can boost productivity while remaining remote.

TikTok recently announced that, starting in September, “it will require most US employees to return to the office five days a week,” according to Business Insider.

But as LinkedIn reports, “Tech and media companies remain somewhat split on the value of RTO: While Instagram and Amazon have forced most staffers back to the office, YouTube, Spotify and Dropbox are sticking with flexible work.”

At first glance, scientific research mirrors this same divide. A study just published in Frontiers in Psychology found that, among 7,700 participants, those working remotely reported higher well-being scores and lower turnover rates on average than hybrid or in-office employees. On the other hand, an influential study of Microsoft employees found that the sudden shift to remote work caused by the pandemic disrupted the way employees communicated, threatening team performance.

It’s a reality most of us have experienced: The harder it is to reach your coworkers, the easier it is to feel bottlenecked on important work. A question that might take moments to answer in person can delay a project for hours or even days.

Clearly, we’re facing both a challenge and an opportunity. If leaders want to experience the benefits of remote work without the downsides, they have to prioritize smarter asynchronous communication. Here are a few strategies to help you stay productive when you’re collaborating with remote teammates.

Stop Sending Messages that Create Another Message

The Golden Rule for asynchronous communication? Ask this question before clicking the send button on any message:

“Can my recipient give me exactly what I need without asking for more information?”

If the answer is no, add more context.

A general rule of thumb is to make sure everyone knows:

  • What you need
  • Why you need it
  • How you need it
  • When you need it

You can remove several communication cycles by communicating this information clearly up front. Do that across all of your interactions, and you’ll quickly find yourself waiting less and accomplishing more.

Streamline Decision Making by Suggesting a Response

The next time you find yourself asking a question like, "Which option do you prefer?" give this a try instead: "Unless I hear otherwise, I'm planning to use Option A. If you disagree, let me know by Thursday."

Obviously, some decisions are too high-stakes for this approach. But it’s a smart way to accelerate communication and demonstrate leadership skills in a way that earns trust over time.

Give Yourself 48 Hours of Buffer with Important Deadlines

Often, what is described as a communication delay is actually the result of poor planning. Both of these problems are fixable, but the solutions are different.

Some projects are last-minute and difficult to get ahead on. But typically, your most impactful objectives will take place over a longer period of time.

When you’re accountable to an important timeline, adjust your thinking and your calendar to make your personal deadline at least 48 hours earlier than the formal deadline. This will give you time to adjust if communication delays bog the project down.

Pay Attention to Time Zones and Vacation Calendars

It’s uniquely frustrating to approach the end of a project and send an email with a few final questions, only to get an OOO message from a key collaborator. As part of your planning, be sure to note the vacation days of any key stakeholders, so you can get their input before they step away. Similarly, it’s important to note where your collaborators live, as time zones can reduce your window for quick communication.

Ravindra Kondekar is a productivity coach and software professional who has spent more than three decades working in the technology industry, obtaining four U.S. patents. For much of his career, he has collaborated from India with U.S.-based teams, despite a roughly 10-hour time gap. The key, he explains, is to design your work so the time difference doesn't even slow you down.

There are ways to make progress visible without requiring anyone to ask for updates. A brief write-up at a regular cadence—daily for fast-moving work, weekly for longer-running work—can provide much of the visibility that physical proximity in an office provides.

Keep it simple:

  • What’s done
  • What’s next
  • Any blockers

Ravindra says, “After decades of working with U.S.-based teams from India, I've found that the time-zone difference can actually become an advantage. While one person is offline, the other can make progress—and when the handoff is designed well, the work can keep moving almost continuously.”

It’s hard to imagine an employer who wouldn’t be excited about that. By focusing less on location and more on communication, we can design a future in which both companies and the people who run them get to thrive.

item.title: 'Polyester' Goes Viral as a New Gen Z Insult
item.description:
Social Media

'Polyester' Goes Viral as a New Gen Z Insult

"Polyester" as an insult may be part of a larger push against fabricated stuff.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • The term "polyester" is being used as an insult for anything that is cheap, poor quality, or unnatural.
  • Polyester has been blended in phrases like a "polyester lifestyle," which is one a poser would present.
  • This polyester trend may be part of a broader desire for more authenticity and higher-quality things.
The "polyester" trend has people seeing through things that are low-quality, low-effort, and fake.
Source: Nicoleta Ionescu / Shutterstock

This insult is kind of about fiber optics, so to speak. If you do something that looks rather shoddy or fake, don't be surprised if someone calls it "polyester"—even though it didn't involve any activewear, fleece, or bedding materials. That's because "polyester" has become a more generic insult for anything that is considered cheap, poor quality, or unnatural. And this use of polyester may be a natural reaction to what's happening with the broader fabric of society right now.

"Polyester" References Have Been Growing on Social Media

These days you can certainly find plenty of "polyester" references woven into different social media posts and replies, especially from Gen Zers. This includes posts about real polyester, like TikTokers raising concerns about how polyester clothing is made from crude oil and discarded plastic bottles and, thus, is composed of plastic and chemicals that could in turn shed onto you and the environment. I have written in Forbes about such pollution concerns and potential negative health effects. Other TikTok posts have been about trying to purge polyester products from their wardrobes, lamenting how difficult it is to find higher-quality fabrics and clothing, and ridiculing social media influencers trying to sell low-quality merch made of polyester.

Then there's the more specific phrase "polyester edit," which really emerged in 2025 to describe videos that look cheap and poorly edited. The videos that first earned this insult were the slew of ones that were hitting social media then and featured a single character like Spider-Man or Iron Man posing in the foreground with a background of different movie scene clips flashing by rapidly in succession. These potentially seizure-inducing polychromatic mixes—or messes—have led to plenty of "polyester edit" comments in response.

"Polyester' Has Come to Mean Low-Quality, Low-Effort, or Low in Authenticity

Quite a few folks, particularly many Gen Zers, have since become quite, shall we say, "polyester-amorous." You can find the word being used in many different forms—ranging from by itself to being part of a polyester-blend phrase. In all cases, the purpose is to label someone or something as low-quality, low-effort, or high in faking.

For example, a "polyester lifestyle" could be the type of lifestyle that a poser would present. You know the lifestyle where an influencer brags about sipping matcha all day, enjoying spectacular views, and getting artificial intelligence to do all his or her work while dropping overused and often disingenuous Silicon Valley slogans like "Move fast and break things." Yet at no time does such an influencer provide real, verifiable evidence of being truly wealthy, productive, or successful in any way. Yeah, social media posts by such an influencer could earn a "polyester lifestyle" or just simply "polyester" in response.

The "Polyester" Trend May Be Part of a Broader Desire for Authenticity

The proliferation of such influencers does exemplify why the term "polyester" might suit the times, so to speak. When describing recent trends like the LARPing and chalance ones in "A Funny Bone to Pick," I have written about the apparent growing hunger for more authenticity. That may stem from the proliferation of "fabricated" and fake stuff, with so many politicians, daters, influencers, business leaders, corporations, and others seemingly trying to pull the polyester over your eyes each and every day.

While it's certainly not new to have people trying to fool you and sell you stuff—including themselves—the shift of many activities from in-person to online may be exacerbating the situation. When things aren't as face-to-face in real life anymore, and there's now even more potentially reality-altering tech available, like filters and artificial intelligence, it can be harder and harder to tell what's real from what's not. Therefore, it shouldn't be too surprising to see people being more suspicious and critical of anything that seems artificial.

The "Polyester" Trend May Also Be Part of a Broader Desire for Better-Quality Things

Another source of this "polyester" trend could be other trends toward mass production, cost-cutting, and the commoditization of different services and products across many different industries. The result may be just more lower-quality stuff out there. I mentioned TikToker complaints about what's happening with the clothing industry. But you can find similar complaints about many other industries, such as the music and entertainment ones churning out more formulaic and fabricated stars and content.

It's also common to hear complaints about how service quality has gone down in different industries such as healthcare and air travel. This could be from the continuing consolidation of such industries, where larger entities can no longer offer the personal touch that smaller ones did. Or the prioritization of short-term profits and stock prices over customer satisfaction. Further exploration may be warranted to better understand and address what's happening.

The "Polyester" Trend May Represent Overall Insecurity and Cautiousness

Regardless, a common thread that seems to be running through this polyester trend and the other aforementioned trends is that of insecurity and cautiousness. A Pew Research Center report cited General Social Survey results that showed how the percentage of Americans who indicated that “most people can be trusted” had dropped from 46 percent in 1972 to 34 percent in 2018. And the 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer revealed that close to seven in 10 people polled feared that leaders of institutions are deliberately misleading the public.

So the greater concern is that many people, companies, and other institutions have essentially worn out their welcome when it comes to trust in what they are offering. And this polyester trend is simply a natural fit for that.

item.title: How (Not) to Deal With Transgressive Leaders
item.description:
Politics

How (Not) to Deal With Transgressive Leaders

An analysis of transgressive leaders' appeal and strategies to curb their influence.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Transgressive leaders enjoy growing support and influence.
  • Evidence suggests transgressive leaders are appealing not despite their transgressions, but because of them.
  • The appeal of transgressive leaders hinges on perceived benefits emanating from their actions.
Source: John Hain / Pixabay

Transgressive leaders are on the rise. News reports regularly feature fraud, racism, hate speech, sexual misconduct, democratic undermining, and other types of violations by leaders—from captains of industry to influencers to presidents of nations.

One might expect such transgressions to be met with sanctions. However, people often turn a blind eye to leaders who violate norms of fairness, honesty, decency, or care. What’s more, the outcomes of political elections across the globe indicate people willingly vote transgressive leaders into office.

Scientific evidence, too, shows that responses to transgressions are less negative than one might intuit. A qualitative study of 246 incidents of norm-violating behavior revealed explicitly negative reactions in only about a third of the cases; in other cases, reactions were neutral, mixed, or even positive.

This is puzzling. Cultures all around the world emphasize the importance of doing good. The value of a virtuous life is highlighted in all major religions. It is reinforced through cultural products, from children’s books to Hollywood movies. Why, then, are transgressive leaders endorsed? Psychological research offers three interrelated answers.

Understanding the appeal of transgressive leaders

First, moral judgments are not absolute; they are malleable and context-dependent. What may seem like basic moral principles are not equally shared by everyone. For example, whereas notions of honesty and equality are central to the worldviews of progressive-liberal individuals, conservative individuals place relatively more value on (cultural) "purity" and loyalty.

Moreover, preferences for moral qualities in others are remarkably elastic. If people stand to gain from another’s transgressions, their preferences can shift from moral to immoral conduct. For instance, people respond more leniently to others’ norm-violating behavior when they derive (financial) gains from that behavior.

Other work shows that preferences for moral versus immoral traits in others depend on one’s current goals. In one study, participants playing the role of defense attorney (whose objective was to secure a non-guilty verdict from a jury) reported greater liking of a merciful rather than a merciless jury member. However, those in the role of prosecuting attorney (whose objective was to secure a guilty verdict) preferred a merciless to a merciful jury member. In other words, when a harsher approach was conducive to people’s goals, their preferences for moral versus immoral traits shifted.

Second, people who break the rules radiate an aura of power and dominance. Breaking rules comes with a risk of backlash. By knowingly flouting rules, people signal they can withstand any repercussions—a sign of power. Indeed, several studies show norm violators are perceived as more powerful and dominant than norm abiders. Such perceptions fit the romance of the "strong leader" and fuel the impression that transgressive leaders get things done.

Transgressive leaders are particularly attractive when their actions (appear to) benefit others. In a series of experiments, participants voluntarily granted power and leadership to another person who exhibited “prosocial” norm violations. For instance, in one study, participants conferred power and control over monetary outcomes to a confederate who stole coffee from the experimenter and also offered them a cup.

Third, research shows that dominant leaders are most attractive in times of economic uncertainty, conflict, and competition, when people tend to look for leaders who can ward off apparent threats. Accordingly, support for transgressive leaders increases in competitive situations. It is no coincidence that autocratic leaders habitually point to the danger of “hostile elements,” such as the independent press, immigrants, or the liberal elite. The greater the perceived threat, the greater the attractiveness of transgressive leaders.

Successful autocrats often spin their transgressions as solving the problems of ordinary people. By fabricating or exaggerating enemy threats, they pave the way for unlawful countermeasures that purportedly eliminate those threats. Thus, they simultaneously suggest a solution to a problem and bolster their perceived effectiveness as leaders by fueling perceptions of dominance and power.

Moralizing alone is ineffective

A common reaction to this spiel is moral outrage, which leads opponents to criticize the immorality of transgressive acts. Understandable as this reaction may be, it is not a sufficient antidote to transgressive leaders. The strategy of moralizing transgressions hinges on the assumption that normative behavior is uniformly appreciated and counternormative behavior frowned upon, but as we have seen, mounting evidence indicates this assumption is incorrect.

Transgressive leaders derive their popularity at least in part from their bald norm defiance, particularly when it appears to benefit others. Thus, although clarifying norms is important, harping on immorality is unlikely to be effective. What’s more, it can backfire as it makes the leader’s behavior seem even more ballsy.

How can we curb transgressive leaders?

If the appeal of norm violators hinges on the apparent utility of their behavior, as accumulating evidence suggests, then the remedy is obvious: debunking the idea that breaking rules solves society's problems. The current analysis suggests two concrete strategies.

First, opponents could dispel the alleged benefits of leaders’ transgressions. While it is typical for transgressive leaders to frame their unlawful behaviors and policies as solutions to pressing problems, their transgressions often do not benefit society; to the contrary, they may damage it. Making that apparent seems critical in counteracting the appeal of transgressive leaders.

Second, opponents could challenge transgressive leaders’ common threat narrative. In the face of competition and conflict, transgressive leaders’ aura of dominance is seen as an asset in fighting off the “enemy.” Alleviating perceptions of conflict should lower transgressive leaders’ allure by reducing the utility of dominance.

In short, evidence suggests transgressive leaders are appealing not despite their deviant behavior, but precisely because of it. This paradoxical insight calls for different ways of dealing with them to uphold humane societies.

item.title: What Forgiveness Is Not and Why
item.description:
Forgiveness

What Forgiveness Is Not and Why

People sometimes reject forgiving because they misunderstand it.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Forgiveness is so rarely discussed in societies that it leaves the gate open for serious misunderstandings.
  • At least nine issues are too often confused with forgiveness, leading people to reject it.
  • Forgiveness is your choice when you are ready, and with the proper understanding of what it is and is not.

When I began studying forgiveness scientifically in 1985, I realized that forgiveness as a research topic had been neglected in psychological research for close to a century. Yes, there were a few journal articles on apology, but no published empirically based studies on people forgiving those who were unjust to them. As I started giving talks on forgiveness, I noticed two trends: (a) as in the psychological sciences, people in the general public rarely had conversations about forgiveness—what it is, how one goes about forgiving, and what occurs upon forgiving, and (b) when people adamantly opposed the idea of forgiving, they were misunderstanding what it actually is.

To help correct that latter point—misunderstanding what forgiveness actually is—the point of this post is to describe nine not-uncommon views of forgiving that are completely incorrect. The hope is that those who react in anger at the word “forgiveness” will first have an opportunity to see what forgiveness is not, so they can make a wise decision about whether to try it.

When people forgive, they are engaging in a moral virtue of willingly offering mercy to those who were unjust to the forgiver (Song et al., 2025). All moral virtues center on goodness. Being fair, for example, is demonstrating the moral virtue of justice in which a person willingly engages in an equal exchange, such as paying a carpenter for a newly constructed table. The goodness of forgiveness centers on having mercy on others because those others are persons, and all persons have worth, not because of what they have done but because of who they are: unique and irreplaceable humans.

Consider the nine misconceptions of forgiveness below.

Source: Serhii Nemyrivskyi / Dreamstime

Forgiveness as Moving on

A common expression for some people is that when they forgive, they are “just moving on” from the situation. Yet, can’t one “move on” with indifference or annoyance toward the offending person? Where, then, is the mercy, the acknowledgment of the inherent worth of the other?

Forgiveness as Excusing

When people “just let it go,” they are saying that what happened was not unjust. Because there was no unfairness, the “forgiver” can just drop the whole issue and not seek justice or offer mercy. After all, if there was no transgression, there is no need to forgive.

Forgiveness as Forgetting

The expression “forgive and forget” gets forgiveness into trouble all the time. I have been confronted with people saying angrily to me, “If I forgive, then might I fail to recall what happened, and so I am vulnerable to the other’s nonsense over and over again?” When we forgive, it usually is out of emotional pain, and we rarely develop a sort of amnesia when it comes to pain. Instead, we remember in new ways, such that when we recall the unjust incident, it passes harmlessly through our heart. We do not forget, but remember in new ways.

Source: Idreamphotos / Dreamstime

Forgiveness as Calming Down

When people see forgiveness only as protecting their own emotions, they can mistakenly equate it with calming down angry emotions. Yet, as you probably can see, this focuses exclusively on the self, not on the one who acted unfairly. If forgiveness is a moral virtue of mercy toward others, then this exclusive focus on one’s own emotions distorts what it is. Yes, people may calm down as they forgive, but that is a consequence of forgiveness, not its essence.

Forgiveness as Reconciliation

This one gets me in trouble all the time. People who equate forgiving and reconciling can say this to me, “How dare you discuss forgiveness with me relative to my ex-partner? Given the abuse I suffered, this could kill me.” Yet, reconciliation is not a moral virtue; it is a negotiation strategy in which two or more people come together in mutual trust. A person can forgive from a distance and not reconcile if the other person cannot be trusted.

Forgiveness as an Abandonment of Justice

Another misunderstanding of forgiveness that strikes fear in the heart is the error that as you forgive, you cannot seek justice. This is “either-or” thinking in which the person falsely believes that only one moral virtue can be offered at any one time. Yet, you can offer moral virtues together. You can be patient and merciful, and ask for fairness from those who are behaving wrongly. Forgive and seek justice.

Forgiveness as Only Saying, “I Forgive You”

While words matter, forgiveness challenges us to plant this moral virtue in the heart, with merciful thoughts and feelings toward the other person. Just saying, “I forgive you,” is too superficial if the person now thinks that forgiveness is all wrapped up in saying this. Words, softened feelings, and thoughts on the inherent worth of the other are all combined in this moral virtue.

Source: Fizkes / Dreamstime

Forgiveness as a Depletion of One’s Emotional Energy

“Come on! I have enough stress in my life, and now you are suggesting that I tackle the new and challenging work of forgiveness? Forget it.” Such a statement can occur when people fail to realize the paradox of forgiving: As people forgive, they tend to refresh as anger lessens, a softened heart emerges, and they can experience considerable emotional healing. See Yu et al. (2021) as just one example of this. People who see forgiveness as energy depletion usually have not tried forgiveness in a scientifically valid way.

Forgiveness of Situations

You cannot forgive situations because you cannot have mercy on them. For example, if a tornado damages your roof, you cannot forgive the tornado because you cannot reach out in mercy and see the inherent worth of this weather event. You cannot have mercy on a flat tire or on the peeling paint on your wall. Forgiveness is for people who have behaved unjustly. When some people think they can or should forgive situations, forgiveness can begin to look trivial to them.

In Conclusion

Source: Evgenyatamanenko / Dreamstime

If you are feeling ambivalent about forgiveness, try first to ascertain if you have been making an error in defining what it is. If not, then perhaps you are not yet ready to do the challenging work of forgiving. You should not feel forced into forgiveness, but instead drawn toward it because you see its value. Forgiveness is your choice when you are ready, and with the proper understanding of what it is and is not.
